rationale: Mentions a corporation funding the ULTIMAC computer but says nothing about answering questions in English; only a loose pointer to a question-answering machine.
A portable voicewrite used to compose letters matches speech-to-text dictation in function, but no recognition mechanism is described.
A machine detecting slight variations in mental activity to read a mind matches brain-activity decoding in function; the mechanism is only vaguely brain-signal sensing.
A "machine-reporter of thoughts and feelings" points toward decoding thoughts, but the fMRI result only reconstructed imagined visual patterns, a much narrower thing.
Controls opening every cell in a country have nothing to do with a patrolling security robot.
A request to get all information on a planet as fast as possible is a generic information query; it hints at retrieval but no system or mechanism appears.
Punching figures into a locator to make a point appear in a galaxy model resembles a computer-driven position display, but it is a model tank, not tracking real-time data.
Robot switchboards and corridor-sweeping robots are service machines, but nothing here serves the public as waiters or greeters do.
A telepathic stare-and-nod "reading mind" has no machine or brain-measurement element.
Telling the ship what you want to do and having it navigate matches voice command in function, but the recognition mechanism is unstated.
Robot-confessors performing a duty hint at robots dealing with people, but the quotation gives no public-service task like serving diners.
A continuously changing 3D star map making the wall look like a miniature universe matches a volumetric 3D display in function, though the mechanism is unspecified.
A ship floating in a sphere of weapons carrying the Brains is not a display of any kind.
Says machine recognition of a face is delicate and would need an enormous Brain, naming the face recognition function; no mechanism and it is treated as infeasible.
Summoning a dicto-typer names a dictation machine that types spoken words, matching the function but with no mechanism.
Dictating a message to a steno-robot matches automatic dictation transcription in function; how it works is not described.
A shielded room like an EEG lab for mind analysis loosely evokes brain-scanning setups but describes no decoding.
Robots automatically controlled by a camp computer over radio matches one computer directing many robots; the Volvo carriers were wired or guided differently and in factories.
Waiters guided by a central robot brain in the basement gives a central computer driving many service robots; the real examples were two stand-alone robots.
The face-recognition remark about a larger Brain does not describe a computer directing a fleet of robots.
A robot scanning a man's features to identify him matches automated face recognition in function, with only a vague scanning mechanism.
Directing the station computer by voice panel to run the precession equipment matches a station computer handling attitude control; voice input is an extra and the context is fictional.
Comparison of a person's speed against a dicto-typer implies a speech-to-text typing machine, but no operation is described.
A vast space-chart overhead is a display of position, but nothing indicates computer-driven live updating.
Lights pulsing and coalescing in an unspecified object does not describe a 3D display.
Android female surrogates shipped to colonies point toward companion robots, but Furby is a toy pet, so the match is loose.
Robots serving as traffic police are a policing robot idea, but the real product was a patrolling warehouse guard, a different job.
Automatically recording a speaker's voice vibration pattern to detect a violation matches voiceprint speaker identification in function; the mechanism is only hinted.
A vocowriter used with a special speaking voice is a voice-to-text device, matching dictation transcription in function.
A tri-dim chart filling much of a room loosely evokes a 3D display, with no detail of how it works.
A machine exclaimed to be "reading my thoughts" points at thought reading but has no mechanism or output form.
Reading a subject's inmost thoughts while he fails to control them is a mind-reading claim only, with no brain-signal mechanism shown.
A delivery section producing an answer facsimile tape after a query matches a question-answering computer in function; START's mechanism of English parsing is not given.
A telepath who knows where something is hidden is a psychic ability, not a machine.
A machine-brain weighing facts to give an unbiased answer hints at answering questions but is not about answering English questions from the public.
Robots to operate and supervise other robots is a hierarchy of control, loosely pointing to central coordination of robots.
Remarks on needing guidance or command for left-behind things say nothing specific about computer-directed robots.
Mentioning that someone might examine retina patterns names retinal identification as a check, matching function; the scanner mechanism is not given.
A picture appearing on a white screen that no one had seen before loosely evokes displaying mental imagery, but nothing says it comes from a mind.
A robot jammed by contradictory orders from a supervisor suggests hierarchical robot command, but a central computer driving carriers is not shown.
A robot barker chattering to lure customers inside is a public-facing robot, but it is a salesman rather than a waiter taking orders.
Mastering a language's grammar and vocabulary quickly hints at accelerated learning, but nothing mentions sleep.
A receptionist robot controlling the inner doors is a robot serving visitors in public, matching the service-robot function though not waiting tables.
A broadcast message that shifts robots' allegiance is a command hijack, not a service robot interacting with the public.
A device resembling a telephone mouthpiece with the brain not acted upon says nothing about detecting mental activity.
A new red dot appearing in a three-dimensional model of space at a planning center matches a 3D volumetric display used for planning, though how it is made is unstated.
A room of cybernetic controls as the nerve center of an automatic building is machine control, not a security robot.
States that the brain emits electrical discharges varying with activity and that machines can detect them; this matches brain-signal sensing, though it stops short of decoding contents.
An "idgit" computing a supply list and wanting service is a computing machine at work, only loosely retrieval.
A helmet put on a man's head to learn what he knows is a head-worn brain-reading device, matching function, with no decoding mechanism given.
Immobile robots tensed for action says nothing about guarding or patrolling.
A transparent globe inflating to four feet over a device matches a volumetric 3D display in form; how it renders imagery is not described.
A woman telling a machine or person what to remember and being obeyed is voice instruction, but with no recognition of speech described.
Coding an unlimited file search for any person matching a description and any information matches computerized retrieval from a database; the tracer input differs from a DIALOG terminal.
An Information Center able to answer any question matches a question-answering system in function; how it works is not described.
A large circular graph with pulsing white lines is a display of some kind, but not clearly computer-fed real-time situation data.
A building-attached robot manager who cannot come is not serving the public.
Taking a kid's retina pattern directly names retinal scanning for identification, matching function; the access-control context is not shown.
A brain holding data on all explored worlds and comparing a landing site against them matches database retrieval and comparison; no query interface like DIALOG.
Questioning someone's dreams hints at probing the mind, with no machine or measurement stated.
Calling for every scrap of data on a planet and receiving a fair amount matches querying a remote database for information; the terminal and phone link are not given.
A shout at a robot to serve mocks a robot waiter but the quotation only gives the command.
Robots whose radio senses tune to those above gives a hierarchy of command, loosely like central coordination.
The destruction of a Master Machine halting everyone suggests central control of many agents, partly matching, though it concerns humans.
All internal functions of a ship, including care of its crew, relegated to robots and automatic machinery matches a computer running a station, though Skylab did far less.
Telelenses reporting back to a Brain beneath the streets matches a central computer taking input from many robots, with only sensing described.
A spoken remark that someone can handle it says nothing about robot control.
Sending out six geepees to a location suggests dispatching robot guards, but their function is unspecified.
A machine holding a person's voice pattern so a name request lets them in matches voice authentication; the context is a gate, not the corporate computer center.
A piano robot leading the orchestra and coordinating other robots matches one unit directing many; the mechanism is musical rhythm, not routing.
Detectors driven through cities to pick up a person's pattern loosely evokes sensing brain patterns, but at a distance and unlike decoding.
Obtaining recordings of chosen material in printed, pictorial or audio form matches information retrieval in function; how searching works is unstated.
Ear-tubes that respond to sound beside memory and tape matches voice input to a computer; recognition of speech is implied but not detailed.
A Menograph that supersedes pen and pencil suggests a writing device, but nothing says it reads thoughts.
A feminine animated dummy carrying a vessel is a humanoid server, but little describes interaction with the public.
The technique of teaching arbitrary knowledge in sleep matches sleep learning in function; no mechanism, and the real result only covered word associations.
Coding a problem, gathering all information, weighing and giving an answer matches a question-answering machine in function; no natural-language parsing.
A cart serving coffee appears to be a service robot, but the quotation shows no voice recognition at all.
A wall scanner checking people against a large store of registered images and data matches automated face recognition; the context is a security checkpoint.
A robot scanning a card and acknowledging is an access check by a machine, loosely a security robot.
A remark about unfinished business after a jump contains nothing about looking up information.
A "thinkwriter" in capable hands loosely names a thought-to-text device, but the quotation describes nothing of how it works.
An electrode clamped to a man's head and plugged into the wall to interrogate him matches brain-signal reading in function; the decoding is not described.
A camera feeding a police main computer that matches a description on file to alert robots matches automated face recognition; the match is against a description, not a stored image.
Saying "Open" to a lock which recognizes the speaker matches voice command and speaker-specific recognition; the context is door access, not terminals.
A robot postal service sorting and delivering mail is a service robot but not one dealing with customers face to face.
Circuits searching storage tubes for a named person's record matches computerized record retrieval; the remote terminal and phone access differ.
Brain electromagnetic vibration used to tell a story matches reading brain signals to get content; the signal type and decoding are different from fMRI.
A memory-prober reading a man's life history from his mind matches mind reading in function, with the mechanism unnamed and far grander.
Two men studying small dots in a tri-di matches a 3D display used for analysis, with no detail on how it works.
Walls of electronic file controls suggest large automated files, but no query or retrieval is described.
A row of automated phono-typers among office equipment names a dictation typing machine only in passing.
Using a stenophone to dictate a reading list matches voice dictation to text in function; no recognition mechanism is mentioned.
A machine recording impressions that affect its later actions matches the learning-machine function; the mechanism is stated vaguely and Hull's was electrochemical.
Speaking directly to the big computer and getting spoken answers matches voice interaction in function, but recognition is not described and the context is a single privileged person.
Recorded words electronically assembled to answer an almost infinite number of questions matches a question-answering system, with canned-word synthesis and no language parsing.
A remark that a device only needed a transformer says nothing about dictation.
Machines that crack any problem into a formula give an answer from a problem statement, a calculation notion rather than answering English questions.
A door announcing a visitor by name is a speaking machine, with recognition of speech not involved.
Everything automatic until a robot or computer calls for help matches a crew relying on onboard computers to run a station; Skylab's computer handled only some tasks.
A small tube held to the eyes with flashes matches retinal scanning in function, though the purpose is not stated.
Little beasts still in the nursery stage are unspecified robots, with no central computer.
Requesting a unit from an Information Bank of a Law and Policy Machine matches a question-answering database; there is no natural-language answering shown.
A robot proctor gripping a man's elbow to lead him away matches a security robot restraining people, with no patrol aspect.
Fixing up the sound receptors and voice for a robot loosely evokes speech input and output hardware.
A being intruding on a mind to get information is mind reading with no instrument involved.
Holding a prepared disk to the eye for twenty seconds to record an eyeprint matches eye-based identification; it is a card-based scan, different from a retinal scanner.
Picking up a lightweight no-back from the ship's library suggests a portable reading device, but not electronic form.
A robot ticket clerk with a camera recording the buyer's face and destination matches a robot serving the public; the sale only mildly like robot waiters.
Voicing a demand for a statistical summary into a mouthpiece and getting it printed at once matches a computerized retrieval of figures; the voice input is an extra.
A red light triggering a flashed number on a board matches an automated position display responding to events, but the system is vague.
Telelenses reporting back to a central Brain are the eyes of robots, but nothing here shows guarding or policing.
Having a mind picked apart layer by layer by a mind-blasting process loosely refers to forced mind reading, with no mechanism.
A machine converting thought into visible form matches displaying imagined content; the quanta idea is not how fMRI works.
Dim formless figures moving across a lit space loosely evokes displayed mental imagery, but nothing ties it to a mind.
Devices designed to answer any question the mind could ask matches a retrieval machine, with only media types named.
Coding and feeding every bit of information to the Brain matches loading a database for later questions; the querying side is absent.
A repeated thinkwriter in capable hands is a writing device with no description of how it takes dictation.
Feeding in coordinates of a space event to a machine is a database query by position, but the text stresses memory and says nothing of the response.
Playing a recording in reverse giving back knowledge in spools suggests knowledge transfer, but not during sleep.
An automatic library with projected index and tape delivered after punching a call number matches a computer-based retrieval system, though it is closer to a stack-access terminal.
A stone that opens the gyro only under its influence is an access token, but not an encoded card read by a machine.
A female wall greeting visitors and asking about an appointment matches a robot receptionist serving the public.
The computer taking over and controlling water flow to orient a wheel's spin axis matches a computer managing a station's attitude control.
Rating computers crediting an audience figure is consumer analytics by computer but about audience size, not credit risk scoring.
Huge punched-card files for records too numerous for human clerks point to mechanized record storage, but no query or retrieval by remote terminal.
An analogue/digital computer in complacent control of overall complexities with automatic accuracy matches a computer running a station, with no specifics.
Inserting a key into a hole that contacts an electronic device for each worker or guard matches an access token read by a machine; a key instead of a card.
Electronically controlled mechanical servants everywhere that look alive are service robots, but nothing shows them serving the public.
Brains picked while unconscious is mind reading by an unknown agent, with no machine mechanism.
A metal rectangle showing the heavens nearby is a position display, but nothing shows computer data feeding it.
Collecting thought as vibrations of electric current directly from the brain matches reading brain signals, though the thought content decoding differs.
A figure with a word-repeater inside that gestures at certain sounds matches sound-triggered response, a keyed-word reaction like early recognizers.
A TV reading machine that uses micro-libraries across America matches remote access to stored information, with television display rather than a terminal.
Devices delicate enough to detect brain waves emitted by the human brain match brain-signal sensing for mind reading, with decoding not described.
A seer saying you will always keep friends is not a robot.
Sound sensors built into robots, keyed to respond to their names and a few simple commands, match limited-vocabulary speech recognition; household context differs.
A nervous-system-like control system through which robots respond to a master machine matches central control of many robots, a conceptual statement.
Absorbing languages and social structure through hypno-tapes suggests learning by recording, with no sleep stated.
A machine that hears questions and answers from billions of microtapes matches a question-answering computer, where speech input is a plus.
A line about keeping machines from computing the truth does not describe answering questions.
A Reacto machine testing everyone's reaction to music is consumer response analysis, loosely like marketing analytics but with no scoring of customers.
Mobile repair units dispatched when scanning fails and an offer to alert the staff match a computer maintaining a station automatically; no statement of attitude control.
A command to take someone to a named unit is a robot guide, with nothing about its operation.
A servo-robot waiter seating diners at a table matches the Pasadena robot waiter; the real ones took orders and served food.
Cars recording statistics, pictures, heights and weights, then correlating the data matches machine profiling of customers, though not credit scoring.
A scanner identifying his insides to open his door matches machine identification for access, using a body scan not a card.
A brainwave pickup receiving a person's pattern constantly is identification by brain signal, which is not a machine-read card.
Getting information from automatic scanners of a city library matches machine information retrieval, with mechanism vague.
Machines answering problems of daily life is a generic claim used to argue for prophecy, with no question-answering mechanism.
A three-dimensional form of flickering light and shadow in the center of a cabin matches a volumetric 3D display; the clinical planning use is absent.
A remark that it depended on what you wished to select does not describe answering questions.
A ship loyal only to its master points to owner-specific control but no voice recognition is shown.
Walking to a tri-dim chart filling the room loosely evokes a large situation display, with no real-time computer.
A machine registrar with personality is a conversing machine, but nothing says it answers questions.
Translating brain waves into pictures matches thought display in function; the mechanism is only "waves" and it is a claimed ability, not a decoded visual pattern.
Deep-probing a mind to learn what someone has thought about hints at mind reading, with no device or method described.
Getting a replacement within seconds from a filing computer implies a stored-item lookup, though it is mostly a parts dispenser.
The bare statement "We know all about you" contains nothing about a device or reading minds.
A robot luggage-carrier following a "bone" is a following service robot, but it does not wait on or speak to the public.
A robotic barkeep serving a drinker matches a robot serving the public in a bar, much like a robot waiter; no mechanism given.
An Oracle that answers any questions promptly and completely matches a question-answering system in function, with no mechanism.
Robot croupiers and dealers who cannot cheat are service robots in a casino, but the quotation has no task like taking orders.
The name "Menograph, or mind-writer" suggests a device that writes thoughts, but the quotation gives no function beyond the name.
Speaking into a mike so robots speed up matches voice command of machines in function; recognition is implied, not described.
Magnified illuminated book sheets on a wall rack are a reading aid, but no electronic content or portable device.
Deleting items from a record tape and its tubes shows stored data being managed, not retrieved.
Summarizing a picture in a tactical tank is a display of a situation, but done by trained telepaths and not computer data.
Gardeners that repel strange robots from entering the park act like guards, loosely a security robot, but are not patrolling like a Sentry.
A machine offering to respond to only one person's questions points at a question-answering device but with no mechanism.
A fad item compared with a ouija board does not describe thought display.
Robots patrolling the streets in anti-crime campaigns match robot police in function; the mechanism of a central Brain and city scale differ.
A ship at the center of weapons carrying Brains is not a display.
A lock keyed to the owner's brain wavelength is machine-checked identity, but it is a brain-wave key, not a readable card.
A door mike following him with its snout and a hi-fi picking a random tape involves microphones but not recognizing speech.
Saying the device cannot detect telepathy is a limit on a brain-reading device with no mechanism.
Telling a machine's microphone the date and time by voice matches speech input to a machine, but there is no recognition stated.
A stroboscope flickering over a blind man's eyes for mind reading loosely involves a head-applied apparatus, without decoding.
A police experimental robot reporting for duty matches a robot in a police role; there is no patrol or machine surveillance.
Robots sent out to do someone's work hint at an agent and its machines, with no central computer.
Putting items in a dream machine at night to start a job next day matches learning during sleep; the mechanism is absent.
A robowaiter approaching with a menu board in metal hands matches the Pasadena robot waiters; the quotation lacks taking orders.
A desk cabinet finding any of three million items in three seconds with neighbors matches rapid database lookup; no remote terminal.
Robots dispatched when scanning fails is a maintenance response with no speech recognition.
